PART I

AFTER VICTORY
SAVA AND NEMI · VAOR · THE NEXT TWO YEARS
The victory at Deaf Lake did not produce peace, but a period in which every institution claimed the emergency would end after the next temporary measure.
Two years after Deaf Lake, the first towers appeared on Arua's surface.
They had no clear function. Weapons could be mounted more safely underground, and solar storms made height a vulnerability. The builders claimed the towers allowed surveillance of the roads. Sava knew drones could observe the roads better.
Their real usefulness was to be seen.
For thousands of generations, nivari had hidden their homes from the sky. Even Ivarra's palaces lay beneath rock, their entrances imitating folds in the terrain. Daran Veyr raised the first tower above Vaor, a brown blade of fossilised root visible to the edge of the Night. He placed the First Face's frontal sign at its summit.
“It's an insult to instinct,” he said at the inauguration. “That's why it's art.”
The other Houses imitated him. Towers became depots, command posts, shrines to the dead and places where young people climbed to prove they could sleep beneath a sky without a ceiling. A new political expression formed around them: the Vertical Houses.
Ivarra called them emergency regimes.
The emergency had already lasted twenty-seven months.
In the registers, the twenty-seven months between the lake and the tower occupied only a few lines: stabilisation, population integration, reconstruction, defensive reorganisation. For those who had lived them, nothing had been stable.
In the first week after victory, Vaor did not know what to do first with survival. The clinics were full, the main pipes worked only a few hours each cycle, and central prisoners received the same food as the fighters who had captured them. That had been Taren's rule. On the third day, a mother came to the Civil Office and asked why the agent who had burned her home received medicine while her son waited.
Sava had no answer that did not resemble cruelty.
“Because he's wounded now,” she said.
“And when was my son?”
“Then he should have received it too.”
“He didn't.”
“I know.”
“Then your equality begins exactly after it would have helped us.”
The woman left before Sava finished explaining the law, prisoners and what kind of people they would become if treatment depended on hatred. In the report, the case appeared as a “dispute over clinical priority”. Sava erased the phrase and entered the woman's question exactly. Daran approved the change, then projected it in a speech about Vaor's nobility. The woman asked him to remove her name. Daran removed the name and kept the pain.
In the second week, demobilisation began. Taren sent home half of those who had fought at the lake. Two days later, three communities asked for their guards back: depots had been attacked, former central agents wandered without food, and groups wearing the Face sign were confiscating things in victory's name. Taren sent temporary patrols and forbade them to stay more than one cycle in the same settlement.
The patrols returned after a cycle, then again. Sleeping places were built for them. A technician was assigned to repair their weapons. A kitchen was allocated exclusively to guard shifts because they could not wait in civilian queues. Every measure was temporary. Together, they formed an institution.
Raal handled recruitment and brought Taren candidates no school would have accepted: over-impulsive youths, women who had defended their alcoves with tools, former thieves who knew the Night roads, central agents who could no longer return to Ivarra. Taren rejected those who demanded rank before training and those who spoke too often of blood.
“You'll keep only the ones who lie better,” Raal told him.
“Then stay and show me which ones they are.”
“I'm an excellent liar.”
“That's why I keep you close.”
In the second month, Daran proposed a Festival of Staying. He wanted enormous cloths, fires on the surface and the dead people's names projected onto rock. Sava showed him the calculation: the ceremony's materials could repair two reservoirs and feed the clinics for nine days.
“People don't live on nutrient alone,” Daran said.
“They die very concretely without it.”
“They need to know what the others died for.”
“The dead no longer need your explanation.”
The ceremony took place anyway, but without fires. Workers hung a piece of burnt pipe at every entrance. Each family wrote its own name, without Daran being able to choose the order. Some pieces carried thanks to the First Face. Others accused Daran, Ivarra, the Chamber or even Taren. One carried only the words: *we don't yet know why*.
For Oru, Nemi chose a green piece cut from the pipe he had opened before dying. She wanted to write “he saved the children”. Sava stopped her.
“He did more than his last act.”
“Then what do I write?”
They stayed a long time beside the crooked root planted at the ceremony. The graft looked sick, but Bes had found a living strand and connected it to a water circuit. Around it, the soil smelled of wet minerals and ash.
Nemi wrote: *Oru Ilen. He repaired what he could touch.*
“It doesn't say he was my father.”
“Those who know you know.”
“But a long time from now?”
Sava thought of all the people reduced in archives to a function or a relationship with someone more important.
“Add that too.”
Beneath the first line, Nemi wrote: *He was my father, and not only that.*
In the fourth month, the children began playing Deaf Lake. Some were agents running across the ice, others Faces striking imaginary valves. No one wanted to be the civilian caught between them. When an instructor tried to introduce the role, the children turned it into the person who brought water after the fighting.
Taren watched once. He saw a boy imitate the way he had raised Oru's rod. The movement was wrong and heroic. He showed him the correct angle, then regretted it. The next day, all the children repeated the gesture better.
“You gave them the lesson they wa

THE WHITE WINTER
SAVA AND SEN · VAOR · SIX YEARS AFTER DARAN'S DEATH
The White Winter came not from climate, but from administration. The orbital mirrors were moved so little that every order seemed technical; after a few months, thousands of families walked east with the ice behind them.
Six years after Daran's death, the light moved.
It did not go out abruptly. The orbital mirrors changed angle by fractions so small that only instruments noticed at first. The Belt's fertile band slid east. Ivarra and the loyal domains received nine more minutes of light each cycle. Vaor, Lur, Orm and the settlements without a House each lost two.
After a month, the soil cooled.
After two, the agricultural bacteria slowed.
After three, the Night's ice entered the first pipes.
Seln Aru called the phenomenon an orbital safety correction. The Great Hearing published models showing instability in the mirror swarm and advised western populations to redistribute temporarily towards the centre. No one uttered the word punishment.
In Vaor, snow covered the bases of the towers.
In Taren's first year of leadership, the position of First Face had been provisional. In the second, the Council renewed it because of local wars. In the third, the Houses requested a five-year mandate to provide “strategic continuity”. Taren accepted after Sava imposed a formal right of removal by three-fifths of the functions. No removal vote had been initiated. The Faces considered him indispensable, the Hands feared the chaos of succession, Memory needed access to military archives, and the Protected had only just formed their representation.
Power had not become hereditary. Time, institutions and fear had simply arranged themselves so the alternative seemed ever more expensive.
Taren no longer lived in Daran's tower. He had turned the upper platform into a coordination hall and slept in a low room beneath the barracks, without windows. Vessa said it was his way of rejecting the symbol while retaining all its commands.
“If you want to prove you aren't the tower's master, move the Council into the workshop,” she had told him.
“The map doesn't fit there.”
“The map fits anywhere. The commanders don't want to sit on the floor beside workers.”
Taren moved two meetings. At the third, the Houses came with their own chairs and guards. A month later, the Council returned to the tower.
The six years had not been quiet. They had merely become organised enough for violence to receive meetings, budgets and deadlines.
In the first year, Sava tried to use the right of removal. Taren had confiscated two House Tel shipments after it refused to send food to a community without a House. The confiscation saved the community's crop and violated the Charter's procedure. Sava requested a vote not because she wanted to remove him, but because an unused rule was not a limit.
The Council met in the workshop at Taren's insistence. The Faces came in armour. The Hands came straight from their shift and smelled of nutrient. Memory projected the complete order. For the first time, the Protected had sent three representatives, one of them Rema, Arel's mother.
“If we remove him, who leads the patrols?” House Orm asked.
“Someone else,” Sava replied.
“Name them.”
There was no name the Houses could agree on. The vote obtained fifty-nine per cent, one point below the threshold. Taren remained.
That evening, the channels announced that the First Face had won a confidence vote. Sava demanded a correction: it had been a failed removal attempt. The correction appeared under the headline “Leadership accepts democratic oversight”. The mechanism meant to show Taren could be removed had demonstrated to the public exactly how hard it was.
“Did you vote against me?” he asked her.
“Yes.”
“Did you think I should go?”
“I thought the possibility had to be real.”
“And if it had succeeded?”
“Then we'd have learned whether we'd built institutions or only dependence.”
Taren did not get angry. That worried her more. He had begun to receive Sava's opposition as proof of his own tolerance.
In the second year, the community of Hes asked to become a House. The refugees no longer wanted to depend on the old families' votes and believed a name would give them land, a Council seat and the right to a Corps. Sava opposed it. Daran was dead, but his model reproduced without him.
“We don't want old blood,” said the woman who had led the agricultural restoration. “We'll elect leadership for five years.”
“And after five?”
“We elect again.”
She was the first leader. The second election never took place: as the term approached, Hes's border was attacked, and the Council extended the mandate for continuity. Her daughter led the defence. The families preferred her as successor because she knew her mother's codes and had been present at negotiations. No one declared the position hereditary. Every practical reason simply settled in the same family.
In the third year, Sen turned four and received his first public assessment. Vessa had refused the neural testing required of Faces' children. Daran no longer existed, but military clinics had kept the protocol. Parents wanted it because good results opened command schools.
“Don't I want to know whether he has Taren's reflex?” Sava asked her.
“I want to know when he's ill,” Vessa replied. “I don't want every peculiarity to become an invitation to a function.”
“If he has it, it'll be noticed anyway.”
“Then at least let him be noticed as a person before being measured as an inheritance.”
At the children's ceremony, Sen did not startle when a gong accidentally fell. The crowd fell silent, then began striking the floor. The child was frightened by their reaction and began to cry. In the images distributed later, the crying had been cut. Only the boy standing still before the sound remained.
Other parents began requesting partners from families with “frontal stability”. The term was not medical. It included lack of flight, robust jaws, rapid healing, fertility and the

THE TRIAL
SAVA · IVARRA · THE FIRST NINE MONTHS OF THE NEW ORDER
Seln's trial was meant to separate the old order from the new. Instead, it showed how many instruments of centralised peace had become indispensable to the very people who defeated it.
Seln Aru's trial lasted nine months and produced six incompatible definitions of peace.
Central agents maintained that veyrin had prevented a lethal attack. Vaor's survivors showed the bodies of those who had died too calm to run. Mirror engineers demonstrated that moving the light had prevented system overload. White Winter refugees described children buried in frozen soil. The Gardens of Kinship families were divided: some demanded punishment, others testified that they feared returning home more than closed gates.
Seln denied no act.
The tribunal had been built in the old census hall. For four centuries, quotas, moves and birth rights had been approved there. Now the officials' tables formed a semicircle, and the place where families had awaited decisions became witness space.
No side had accepted the panel's initial name. The Houses wanted “the Court of Liberation”. The old agents proposed “the Continuity Commission”. Mist survivors demanded “the Judgement of the Dead”. Sava insisted on a weaker formula: Mixed tribunal for acts of administration and conflict. Everyone hated it, confirming for her that it was sufficiently untriumphant.
The panel had one magistrate from Ivarra, one from Vaor, two elected representatives of affected communities and one Memory member; Sava presided. Taren was not part of it. The Custodianship provided security and could execute the sentence, but his key did not open the evidence archive. Nemi had designed the separation and published the code. In the first weeks, people assumed it was a gesture of trust. Later they understood it had been a gesture of distributed distrust.
Seln came without cloak or restraints. He had lived seven months in the Gardens, in a home identical to those occupied by House families. He had access to books, an inner courtyard and a wall that turned opaque when he approached the exit. He had grown thin. Every morning, he tended his own nutrient plants and sent the tribunal notes on procedural errors in his trial.
“Are you preparing your appeal?” Nemi had asked at one hearing.
“I'm preparing the institution that will need to judge someone else after me.”
“You assume you'll remain useful.”
“No. I assume you'll remain capable of mistakes.”
The first month was devoted to the mist in Vaor. Engineers explained that veyrin had been developed for evacuations and riots in enclosed spaces. It reduced aggression, slowed breathing and made groups easy to direct. At official doses, mortality was below one in a thousand. In Vaor, damaged filters, panic, fires and overcrowding had turned the percentage into seventeen hundred bodies.
A defence lawyer presented the alternative model: if agents had entered with lethal weapons, probable deaths were three times higher. The hall murmured. A woman whose partner had died in the mist stood and threw a piece of breathing membrane towards the table.
“He wasn't a probability,” she said.
The Ivarra magistrate demanded her removal. Sava refused.
“If the tribunal can't bear the sentence, it can't evaluate the model,” she said.
The woman remained. At the end, she testified that she too had advised neighbours to enter the chamber where they died, because central instructions said it was safe. When the lawyer asked whether she considered herself responsible, she began crying.
“That's the wrong question,” Sava intervened. “The witness had no access to data withheld by command.”
“Yet she carried out an instruction,” the lawyer said.
Sava looked at Seln. He did not react. The trial was already becoming a struggle over the line between decision and obedience.
In the third month, Mera Sol testified. She was very old; a frame supported her sails, and her voice came through an amplifier. She had been Taren's therapist and signed the Adaptive Reserve recommendation.
“Did you know he was being tracked as a rare individual?” Nemi asked from Memory's bench.
“Yes.”
“Did you tell him?”
“No. He was a child.”
“Did you tell Sava?”
“I had no permission.”
“Did you oppose using him?”
With her lateral eyes, Mera searched for a point no longer in the hall.
“I opposed authority over others. I recommended technical work, emergency teams, environments where delayed flight could save lives. I thought I was offering him a way to exist without being fully normalised.”
“You sent him towards dangerous places.”
“Yes.”
“For his good or the system's?”
“At the time, I didn't separate the questions.”
Taren watched from the back row. He had not spoken to Mera since leaving for Vaor. After the hearing, he waited for her in the corridor.
“You knew,” he said.
“I knew part of it.”
“When you told me my difference could be useful, you weren't trying to help me. You were preparing me.”
“I was trying to do both.”
“You can't.”
“Parents do. Teachers do. You do it with Sen.”
Taren turned his body face-on. Mera did not retreat.
“I tell him who I am,” he said.
“You tell him who you want him not to become. That's an equally powerful form of shaping.”
Taren left without saying goodbye. That evening, he asked Sen to choose for himself whether to keep attending training. The boy asked whether refusal would change how he looked at him. Taren could not promise it would not.
The fourth month concerned the White Winter. Maps showed the mirrors moving in small steps, each justified by protection of central crops. Engineers demonstrated that no individual command had created the catastrophe. The catastrophe emerged through accumulation and because affected regions had no key to challenge it.
A refugee delegation brought containers of frozen soil. They placed them before the tribunal and recited the names of children who had not reached Vaor. At the eighty-third name, the central magistrate requested a break.
“How much of this

THE SON WITHOUT FEAR
TAREN AND SEN · TWILIGHT BELT · THE NEXT EIGHT YEARS
The return of peace did not abolish the warriors. It moved them into schools, families, examinations and rituals. In eight years, what had been a rare deviation became the model by which a generation measured its maturity.
Sen joined the Face Corps at nine. Taren had forbidden him to use the family name in the examination. All the examiners recognised him by his burn and by the way he did not flinch.
The examination took place in a room without insignia, below the level of the old Chamber. Candidates entered alone. Their names were concealed, and the assessors saw only their age, medical condition and assigned number. Taren had requested this procedure after Sen announced that he wanted to join the Face junior programme. He said his son had to pass through the same door as everyone else.
On the morning of the examination, half the assessors recognised him by his burn before the door closed. The others recognised him by the way he held his body: facing forward, motionless, his sails trimmed shorter than those of civilian children. At nine, Sen already wore a version of the uniform, although the regulations required neutral clothing.
The first test was the old saryx shadow. The system projected movement, scent and low frequencies; the child had to choose between shelter, warning and confrontation. Most candidates fled first, then corrected their course. Sen stayed. He drew his training blade and struck the point of light where the wing joint would have been.
The assessors noted *rapid decision under stress*. None wrote that the boy had seen a real saryx kill Raal, and that his response might be memory, not aptitude.
The second test placed three doors and a group of virtual children before him. Behind one was an attacker; behind another, a fire; the third led to a safe tunnel too narrow for everyone. There was no complete solution. The examination measured the order in which the candidate asked questions, not only the choice.
Sen requested access to the ventilation system, the exact number of children and the time before the fire spread. When the assessor said the data was unavailable, he asked who had withheld it.
“That is not relevant,” replied the woman behind the screen.
“Then the attacker may be the institution that designed the test.”
A laugh in the room was quickly stifled. Sen chose the safe tunnel, divided the group by body size and stayed behind the others. Two virtual children died. He asked to repeat the test with a different distribution.
“The test is over,” the assessor said.
“Then you do not find out whether I have learned.”
At the end, he received one of the highest scores in the cohort. Taren read the report and noticed the comments: *command profile*, *tolerance of loss*, *spontaneous identification with responsibility*. No paragraph mentioned his name. In the confidential appendix, however, appeared: *probable continuity of the Ilen line; high symbolic value.*
“Invalidate the examination,” Taren told the director.
“We cannot invalidate a performance because the assessors know who the candidate is.”
“Then it was not anonymous.”
“No procedure can make society forget a scar.”
Sen was listening beside the door.
“Did I pass?” he asked.
Taren turned towards him.
“You passed a test designed by people who wanted to see you pass.”
“That is not my fault.”
“No.”
“Then will you let me?”
Taren looked at the small uniform, the burn and Raal’s necklace beneath the collar.
“Yes.”
Sen smiled. For him, all his father’s warnings disappeared into that word.
Vessa was waiting outside. She congratulated him and asked him to come for a medical examination the following week. When the boy left to join his classmates, she turned to Taren.
“You tried to remove his name from the examination and left him his statue,” she said.
“He has no statue.”
“He has a living one. It walks through the city and leads the Custodianship.”
“What should I have done? Forbidden him?”
“No. You should have stopped pretending that an equal door corrects the different roads leading to it.”
Taren did not answer. In the years that followed, he would repeat that Sen had earned every rank. It was true. It was not the whole truth.

The junior programme combined schooling with service. The children learned ecology, repairs, history and bodily control. Each week, they spent a cycle in civilian institutions: warehouses, clinics, archives, farms. The idea had been Sava’s. She wanted the Faces to understand that the world did not begin at the edge of a weapon.
In his first year, Sen worked at a moss farm in Ivarra. His task was to clean the fine channels without breaking the nutrient filaments. He was slow and bad at it. A Hands girl, Deli, showed him how to feel the pressure with his fingers.
“You do not push everything that refuses to move,” she said.
“I am not pushing.”
“The channel says otherwise.”
He tried again. By the end of the day, he was breaking fewer roots than that morning. The instructor gave him an average score. In the public report, the episode appeared as evidence of the Custodian’s son’s humility. Deli was not mentioned.
“Tell them she taught me,” Sen insisted.
“We do not control the reports,” the instructor replied.
Sen went to Memory and submitted the correction. Nemi accepted it. The recording became popular: the young Face acknowledging his Hands teacher. Deli received an invitation to the academy, but her family needed her at the farm, and she declined. Sen did not find out until years later. In the story, equality had worked.
At twelve, he was sent on a transport patrol, officially as an observer. Nivari matured quickly, and the crisis generations had driven the age of service lower still. Sen’s body was almost adult; his judgement was not.
The convoy was taking food to an unregistered community at the edge of Night. The locals had stolen two wagons the previous season, and the Custodianship had classified them as a risk. The

THE CHILDREN WHO LOOK AT THE SKY
NEMI · IVARRA · THIRTY-FOUR YEARS AFTER TAREN
Thirty-four years after Taren’s death, peace was stable again, institutions old again, and children again convinced the world had always been this way. Then, from outside the system, came something that belonged to no nivar story.
Thirty-four years after Taren’s death, the children no longer knew how to flee properly.
Nemi noticed this during a lesson in the Low Square. The instructor projected a saryx shadow over the group, and the children scattered too little, in almost straight lines. Some turned to face it before finding shelter. Two ran towards the mechanism to see whether they could bring it down.
By the old criteria, almost all would have been easy prey.
By the new ones, the instructor congratulated them.
They were taller than Sava’s generation. Their hind limbs remained strong, but their shoulders had broadened through selection and training. Their auditory sails were shorter, sometimes through heredity, often cut in the first year so they could not be seized in combat. Their eyes still sat to the sides, but the Custodianship’s clinics offered a convergence correction for Face lines, making frontal focus easier at the cost of part of the peripheral field.
Vessa had called the operation “necessary blindness”. She had died before seeing how popular it became.
Nemi was fifty-six and had few original organs left. Her joints had been replaced, her blood filtered through engineered bacteria, and her sails supported by fine rods. The Memory Corps kept her alive because no archive had managed to classify all the contradictions in her head.
Officially, she was Keeper of the First Recording.
Unofficially, she was the last person who remembered Oru’s smell.
The square had been rebuilt after the siege. Where the first saryx fell now stood a statue of Taren, facing forward, carbon rod in hand. The sculptor had made his sails shorter and his shoulders broader than they had been. At its base, the inscription read: HE CHOSE TO STAY.
Seven times, Nemi had requested the addition: AFTER, FOR A MOMENT, NOT KNOWING HOW TO RUN.
The Council had rejected the wording as a diminishment of historical will.
The lesson did not end with the shadow. After the exercise, the instructor had the children follow the mechanism, identify its joints and propose ways to neutralise it. The two who had run towards the projector received extra points. The child who had found shelter fastest was asked why he had abandoned the group.
“That is what the old protocol says,” he replied.
The instructor projected the protocol: lateral dispersal, sudden changes of direction, use of low tunnels. The movements had been perfected over millennia and had saved entire generations. The children laughed when they tried to imitate them. Their bodies, heavier at the shoulders and trained to face forward, no longer turned easily. One tripped over his own hind limbs.
“This was our ancestors’ response,” the instructor said. “It suited a world in which they could not control the predator. We learn to choose.”
Nemi, seated at the edge of the square, raised a sail.
“Flight was also a choice when there was somewhere to run.”
The instructor recognised her and immediately changed his tone.
“Of course, Keeper. I am speaking of an expanded freedom of response.”
“Then teach them the old response too, until they can perform it.”
“The curriculum classifies it as motor heritage, not a current competency.”
“A body does not preserve heritage through definitions.”
The children watched her. To them, Nemi was almost an archive piece: very old, supported by rods, with long sails that fashion had abandoned. A boy came closer and asked whether she had ever fled a real saryx.
“Not fast enough,” she said.
“Did you kill it?”
“No.”
“Who did, then?”
“My uncle.”
“Taren?”
“Yes.”
“Why did you not learn from him to stay?”
Nemi looked at the statue. The bronze showed Taren alone, blade raised. Nemi remembered the square full of bodies, Sava shouting, Nemi as a child beneath a table, Taren frozen for a fraction before he acted.
“I learned that sometimes someone has to stay,” she answered. “Not that everyone has to want the same thing.”
The child looked disappointed. School questions had answers with clear signs. Her memories added edges.
The instructor resumed the exercise and, this time, made them flee according to the old protocol. The children collided, laughed and asked to repeat the frontal fight. Nemi recorded the attempt. She knew that, a few years later, the clip might be used as evidence of flight’s uselessness, not of a lack of training.
After the lesson, she crossed the Low Square. Ivarra was no longer the city in which she had grown up. The underground levels still existed, but towers rose through the protective membranes towards the sky. Magnetic fields reduced the radiation. Transparent lifts carried residents to the surface for work, ceremonies and walks. Open space, once a punishment, had become a sign of rank.
In the old markets, traders sold eye corrections, shoulder prostheses and decorative sail trimming. Clinics promised “command vision”. Parents brought healthy children to have their peripheral vision reduced before the academy.
Vessa had fought the operation until her final years. She had published studies of accidents caused by the loss of lateral vision, sleep disorders and depression among those modified too early. The Custodianship had introduced consent at adulthood. Families had responded with “gradual correction” programmes beginning in childhood, small enough for each intervention to appear reversible.
When Vessa died twenty years earlier, the Faces had given her a military funeral for her contribution to field medicine. Her genetic criticism had been mentioned in an appendix. Nemi kept her last message in the archive: *I did not lose because the data was weak. I lost because every effect appeared after the reward that produced it.*

EXPANDED AND REVISED EDITION
“Peace does not eliminate selection. It only moves the place where it happens.”
A GUIDE TO THE WORLD
Term
Meaning at the beginning of the novel
Arua
a tidally locked world, with one hemisphere scorched by light and the other frozen; abundant life survives in the Twilight Belt between them.
The Nivari
a social, fertile species acutely sensitive to danger; they have lateral eyes, mobile auditory sails, powerful hind limbs and cities dug or grown beneath rock.
The Long Quiet
four centuries without war, maintained through the rotation of the provincial Houses, restrictions on weapons, the management of births and central control of food, light and infrastructure.
The Great Hearing
a computing network that correlates the cities’ vibrations, population registers, production and ecological models; it makes recommendations, and institutions often claim merely to carry them out.
The Chamber of Measure
the institution that allocates birth rights and the Belt’s resources.
Ivarra and Vaor
respectively, the central capital of peace and a border domain where yields are falling, the population is concealed and the old answers no longer suffice.

Sava Ilen — a demographer in the Chamber of Measure; she believes in the necessity of limits but knows their administrative cruelty.
Oru Ven — Sava’s partner and an engineer of the root network; he regards peace as an ecosystem to be repaired, not revered.
Nemi — their daughter; sensitive to sound, curious and close to her uncle.
Taren Ilen — Sava’s younger brother; diagnosed in childhood with a delayed flight reflex.
Seln Aru — the Custodian of Ivarra; he defends the planetary order with a lucidity that rarely presents itself as violence.
Daran Veyr — the lord of Vaor; cultivated, provocative and convinced that the centre turns the death of the provinces into procedure.
Vessa Dahr — a doctor serving Vaor’s unregistered communities.
Raal — a leader of nivari struck from the registers and driven towards the galleries of the Night.

PART I

PEACE BENEATH THE STONE
SAVA · IVARRA · THREE DAYS BEFORE THE FESTIVAL OF RETREAT
For four centuries, Ivarra had known no war. In that peace, everything dangerous had either been removed from the world, moved into a museum, or renamed a procedure.
Sava Ilen woke before the morning signal, both auditory sails raised and her heart racing at a sound she could not locate.
She lay motionless in the sleeping niche. In Ivarra’s homes, the walls were not entirely rigid. The ceramic root from which they had been grown retained a calculated elasticity, so that footsteps, blows and serious faults could be felt through the bones before they reached the ears. The floor was now sending her small, rapid vibrations. Not an alarm. Not a collapse. More like one light object striking another, with a persistence that belonged only to children.
Sava climbed down from the niche and opened the room’s panel.
Nemi stood barefoot in the shared gallery, her festival ribbon hanging over one eye. She was trying to strike the floor three times without her bone toy jumping out of a chalk circle.
“Shadow, shelter, silence,” the little girl said. “But if I strike too slowly, the instructor says the predator hears me between the beats.”
“The predator is a sheet of cloth pulled along a wire.”
“In the drill. In ancient times it was real.”
Nemi was six standard years old, an age at which a nivar could read, calculate simple rations and generate enough worry for three adults. Her lateral eyes followed the chalk circle and her mother’s expression at the same time. Her long sails trembled at every sound in the pipes. The medical system called this sensitivity auditory hyperreactivity. Oru called it an abundance of attention. Sava, who had access to the complete file, called it nothing at all.
“Go back to bed,” she said. “The signal hasn’t come.”
“Taren isn’t asleep.”
Sava turned one sail towards her brother’s room. No breathing, no rustle. The bed was empty.
“How do you know?”
“His door doesn’t smell of sleep.”
The smells of families mingled in the city’s narrow spaces: baked root, warm down, tool oil, the sweet secretion parents used to mark their children in crowds. Nemi was right. Cold gallery air was coming from Taren’s room.
Oru appeared from the kitchen with a cup between his teeth and two plates in his hands. The short fur on his forearms was stained green with nutrient, though he had washed before sleeping. Root-network engineers wore their work in their skin more than they wore uniforms.
“He’s gone to startle training,” he said. “He left me a message.”
“At this hour?”
“The machines are more convincing when the body hasn’t fully woken up.”
Sava took the cup he held out to her. The infusion was bitter and too hot.
“Does that seem normal to you?”
“No. But normality is precisely what they’re treating him for.”
Oru sat on the floor, his back against the curved wall. Nivari could use chairs, but few preferred them. A body raised above the floor lost the information carried by vibrations, and four centuries had not been enough to make that loss comfortable.
Nemi slipped between them and took a slice of baked root.
“Taren says the machine gets scared faster than he does.”
“Taren says a lot of things when he doesn’t want to answer,” Sava said.
“Do you always answer?”
Oru lowered one sail to hide a smile.
“Your mother answers in tables,” he said. “If the question won’t fit in a table, she puts it in the next cycle.”
Sava nudged a tool he had left on the floor towards him with her foot.
“And your father repairs imaginary pipes during meals.”
Oru was already watching a projection above his wrist. The supply network in the western Belt appeared as a pale branching structure. Three nodes blinked yellow.
“They’re not imaginary. Vaor has lost pressure again.”
“Vaor loses pressure every cold season.”
“Not in the same pipes. The deposits are moving towards the centre.”
“Send the report to infrastructure.”
“I’ve sent it four times. The Great Hearing says the readings are still within the compensation range.”
“Then they are.”
Oru switched off the projection and looked at her with his whole attention. For a nivar, this meant turning the head almost squarely towards someone and giving up half the field of vision. The gesture could be tender or aggressive. With Oru, it was usually a request that she stop hiding inside her profession.
“When did you start talking about the system as though it were the weather?” he asked.
“When I found out how many things break if every official thinks they’re cleverer than the model.”
“And how many break when no one does?”
Nemi looked from one to the other, chewing slowly. Sava did not want the little girl to turn every minor disagreement into a danger signal. She lowered her voice.
“After the Festival, I’ll read the raw data. I promise.”
“You said that after the last Festival too.”
“I didn’t promise then.”
Oru accepted the distinction with a movement of his sail. The morning signal came through the floor: two low pulses, then one long one. The city woke around them. Doors slid open. Water began flowing through the washing pipes. Somewhere a child cried, another laughed, and the footsteps of thousands of inhabitants gathered into a murmur carried through the building’s roots.
The peace of Ivarra had a sound. It was not silence. It was the predictable noise of bodies that knew where they had to go.
•   •   •
The Reflex Therapy Centre occupied an old level of the city, built before ceilings had been lowered to the height considered reassuring. The training room therefore seemed too vast. The lights were buried in the floor, and above them lay darkness. Machines hung there like animals that had not yet learned to come down.
Taren stood in the middle of the circle, his hind paws apart and his arms at his sides.
A mechanical arm shot out from the left. He should have crouched before he saw it fully. Taren turned his head, followed the joint, noticed the wear at the gripping end, and only then took a step.

THE CHAMBER OF MEASURE
SAVA · IVARRA · THE THIRD DAY AFTER THE ATTACK
The Chamber of Measure preserved peace through a simple and impossible arithmetic: each permitted life had to occupy the place of a life ended or a harvest still uncertain.
The Chamber of Measure did not forbid births. It placed them in the future.
That was the official wording and, on most days, Sava managed to believe it. Arua could not be made larger. To the east, living tissue cooked in the open air, and water boiled in the surface fissures. To the west, gases froze in hollows and winds carried needles of solid nitrogen. Between them lay the Belt: a fertile strip seven thousand kilometres long, maintained by orbital mirrors, geothermal channels and a demographic discipline older than every building in Ivarra.
Each family received the right to a first birth. The second depended on deaths, root yields, space available in the depths and the region’s genetic diversity. A third was rare. A fourth existed only in the provinces’ obscene songs.
Nivari generally lived between fifty and sixty standard years and matured quickly. Without predators and restrictions on births, the models showed that the population would double every six years. Within a single lifetime, the Belt would become a hungry mass driven towards fire and ice.
Peace meant more than the absence of death. It meant administering those who were not yet allowed to exist.
On the morning after the Festival, Sava received two hundred and eighty-four applications. The system had sorted them by urgency, which usually meant by the likelihood that the applicants would cause a scene.
The first to enter were two growers from the South Root district. The woman was visibly pregnant, though their permit had been deferred for four years. She kept her auditory sails tightly folded and breathed through her mouth so as not to smell the office’s antiseptic.
“We’re not asking for an exception,” her partner said. “We’re asking for it not to be called a violation.”
“A deferral was issued,” Sava replied. “You acknowledged receipt.”
“We acknowledged that we’d read it. Her body acknowledged nothing.”
The woman looked up. Nivari eyes did not meet easily; to look directly, they had to turn almost the whole head. Her gesture was therefore more brutal than an accusation.
“When we received the first deferral, I was twelve,” she said. “At the second, I was fifteen. Now I’m nineteen. I may have six more years in which I can give birth. How much future must we be given before it becomes a form of no?”
Sava opened the file. The couple’s genetic prospects were good. But the southern districts’ food reserves were below the threshold, and seven hundred births had been moved to the next cycle.
“The child will not be taken away,” she said. “No law allows that.”
Her partner gave a short laugh.
“Of course. We’ll only lose our housing rights, our extra ration and our trades. The child will stay with us while we’re moved towards the edge of the Night. Very peaceful.”
Sava felt one of her sails turning towards the door. Her body was assessing the exit, though there was no danger. She forced her attention back.
“I can reclassify the pregnancy as documented contraceptive failure. You’ll receive a labour sanction, not relocation.”
“It wasn’t a failure,” the woman said. “We wanted it.”
“Then I can’t help you.”
“You can help us. You don’t want to lie to the system.”
“The system isn’t a person I can lie to.”
“Then why are you sitting here?”
After they left, Sava kept the file open. She changed a nutrient-absorption parameter and sent it through the model again. The application went from red to yellow. Probable contraceptive failure. A sanction of a hundred and twenty hours of public maintenance.
The growers left behind two wisps of grey down and the sweet smell of a pregnancy approaching term. Sava called up the next file, but the system asked her to confirm the sanction. The cursor pulsed above the word *intentional*.
She changed it to *probably accidental*.
In the Chamber of Measure, mercy had no field of its own. It had to be entered as measurement error, data loss or sample contamination. Good officials learned to falsify just little enough for the whole to remain true. Perfect officials no longer noticed they were doing it.
Sava remembered her first day at work. She had been thirteen and was still in mourning for her parents. Her mentor, Lio Marr, had shown her the map of the Belt and told her to look at the red points.
“Each one is someone we say no to,” he had explained. “If we cannot bear that, we’ll say yes to everyone, and in twenty years there will be no one left to say anything to.”
At the time, the sentence had seemed mature. Now it seemed only a blade kept well sharpened.
The rest of the morning left her no time to think about her mentor. The Chamber called the next applicants, and the wall projected a family so large that the silhouettes had to be shrunk to fit.
They called themselves the House of Cloth, though they belonged to no political House. Twelve adults lived together on a mushroom farm, raised eighteen children and were requesting four births in the same cycle. The eldest of them spoke: Yara, with broad sails and down cut short from working among spores.
“Your model treats us as twelve separate pairs,” she said. “We share food, sleep and care. A child doesn’t lose a parent when there are eleven others around.”
“The model treats consumption,” Sava replied. “Four simultaneous pregnancies reduce your production at precisely the time your needs increase.”
“Then we rearrange our shifts.”
“You’ve had two deficits in the past five years.”
“Because the city sent diseased spores and called it harvest variation.”
The official beside Sava opened the history. Yara was right: the loss had been assigned to the farm, though it came from a contaminated central batch. If the error was corrected, the family met the threshold for three births, not four.

Officially, she was Keeper of the First Recording.
Unofficially, she was the last person who remembered Oru’s smell.
The square had been rebuilt after the siege. Where the first saryx fell now stood a statue of Taren, facing forward, carbon rod in hand. The sculptor had made his sails shorter and his shoulders broader than they had been. At its base, the inscription read: HE CHOSE TO STAY.
Seven times, Nemi had requested the addition: AFTER, FOR A MOMENT, NOT KNOWING HOW TO RUN.
The Council had rejected the wording as a diminishment of historical will.
The lesson did not end with the shadow. After the exercise, the instructor had the children follow the mechanism, identify its joints and propose ways to neutralise it. The two who had run towards the projector received extra points. The child who had found shelter fastest was asked why he had abandoned the group.
“That is what the old protocol says,” he replied.
The instructor projected the protocol: lateral dispersal, sudden changes of direction, use of low tunnels. The movements had been perfected over millennia and had saved entire generations. The children laughed when they tried to imitate them. Their bodies, heavier at the shoulders and trained to face forward, no longer turned easily. One tripped over his own hind limbs.
“This was our ancestors’ response,” the instructor said. “It suited a world in which they could not control the predator. We learn to choose.”
Nemi, seated at the edge of the square, raised a sail.
“Flight was also a choice when there was somewhere to run.”
The instructor recognised her and immediately changed his tone.
“Of course, Keeper. I am speaking of an expanded freedom of response.”
“Then teach them the old response too, until they can perform it.”
“The curriculum classifies it as motor heritage, not a current competency.”
“A body does not preserve heritage through definitions.”
The children watched her. To them, Nemi was almost an archive piece: very old, supported by rods, with long sails that fashion had abandoned. A boy came closer and asked whether she had ever fled a real saryx.
“Not fast enough,” she said.
“Did you kill it?”
“No.”
“Who did, then?”
“My uncle.”
“Taren?”
“Yes.”
“Why did you not learn from him to stay?”
Nemi looked at the statue. The bronze showed Taren alone, blade raised. Nemi remembered the square full of bodies, Sava shouting, Nemi as a child beneath a table, Taren frozen for a fraction before he acted.
“I learned that sometimes someone has to stay,” she answered. “Not that everyone has to want the same thing.”
The child looked disappointed. School questions had answers with clear signs. Her memories added edges.
The instructor resumed the exercise and, this time, made them flee according to the old protocol. The children collided, laughed and asked to repeat the frontal fight. Nemi recorded the attempt. She knew that, a few years later, the clip might be used as evidence of flight’s uselessness, not of a lack of training.
After the lesson, she crossed the Low Square. Ivarra was no longer the city in which she had grown up. The underground levels still existed, but towers rose through the protective membranes towards the sky. Magnetic fields reduced the radiation. Transparent lifts carried residents to the surface for work, ceremonies and walks. Open space, once a punishment, had become a sign of rank.
In the old markets, traders sold eye corrections, shoulder prostheses and decorative sail trimming. Clinics promised “command vision”. Parents brought healthy children to have their peripheral vision reduced before the academy.
Vessa had fought the operation until her final years. She had published studies of accidents caused by the loss of lateral vision, sleep disorders and depression among those modified too early. The Custodianship had introduced consent at adulthood. Families had responded with “gradual correction” programmes beginning in childhood, small enough for each intervention to appear reversible.
When Vessa died twenty years earlier, the Faces had given her a military funeral for her contribution to field medicine. Her genetic criticism had been mentioned in an appendix. Nemi kept her last message in the archive: *I did not lose because the data was weak. I lost because every effect appeared after the reward that produced it.*

PEACE BENEATH THE STONE
SAVA · IVARRA · THREE DAYS BEFORE THE FESTIVAL OF RETREAT
For four centuries, Ivarra had known no war. In that peace, everything dangerous had either been removed from the world, moved into a museum, or renamed a procedure.
Sava Ilen woke before the morning signal, both auditory sails raised and her heart racing at a sound she could not locate.
She lay motionless in the sleeping niche. In Ivarra’s homes, the walls were not entirely rigid. The ceramic root from which they had been grown retained a calculated elasticity, so that footsteps, blows and serious faults could be felt through the bones before they reached the ears. The floor was now sending her small, rapid vibrations. Not an alarm. Not a collapse. More like one light object striking another, with a persistence that belonged only to children.
Sava climbed down from the niche and opened the room’s panel.
Nemi stood barefoot in the shared gallery, her festival ribbon hanging over one eye. She was trying to strike the floor three times without her bone toy jumping out of a chalk circle.
“Shadow, shelter, silence,” the little girl said. “But if I strike too slowly, the instructor says the predator hears me between the beats.”
“The predator is a sheet of cloth pulled along a wire.”
“In the drill. In ancient times it was real.”
Nemi was six standard years old, an age at which a nivar could read, calculate simple rations and generate enough worry for three adults. Her lateral eyes followed the chalk circle and her mother’s expression at the same time. Her long sails trembled at every sound in the pipes. The medical system called this sensitivity auditory hyperreactivity. Oru called it an abundance of attention. Sava, who had access to the complete file, called it nothing at all.
“Go back to bed,” she said. “The signal hasn’t come.”
“Taren isn’t asleep.”
Sava turned one sail towards her brother’s room. No breathing, no rustle. The bed was empty.
“How do you know?”
“His door doesn’t smell of sleep.”
The smells of families mingled in the city’s narrow spaces: baked root, warm down, tool oil, the sweet secretion parents used to mark their children in crowds. Nemi was right. Cold gallery air was coming from Taren’s room.
Oru appeared from the kitchen with a cup between his teeth and two plates in his hands. The short fur on his forearms was stained green with nutrient, though he had washed before sleeping. Root-network engineers wore their work in their skin more than they wore uniforms.
“He’s gone to startle training,” he said. “He left me a message.”
“At this hour?”
“The machines are more convincing when the body hasn’t fully woken up.”
Sava took the cup he held out to her. The infusion was bitter and too hot.
“Does that seem normal to you?”
“No. But normality is precisely what they’re treating him for.”
Oru sat on the floor, his back against the curved wall. Nivari could use chairs, but few preferred them. A body raised above the floor lost the information carried by vibrations, and four centuries had not been enough to make that loss comfortable.
Nemi slipped between them and took a slice of baked root.
“Taren says the machine gets scared faster than he does.”
“Taren says a lot of things when he doesn’t want to answer,” Sava said.
“Do you always answer?”
Oru lowered one sail to hide a smile.
“Your mother answers in tables,” he said. “If the question won’t fit in a table, she puts it in the next cycle.”
Sava nudged a tool he had left on the floor towards him with her foot.
“And your father repairs imaginary pipes during meals.”
Oru was already watching a projection above his wrist. The supply network in the western Belt appeared as a pale branching structure. Three nodes blinked yellow.
“They’re not imaginary. Vaor has lost pressure again.”
“Vaor loses pressure every cold season.”
“Not in the same pipes. The deposits are moving towards the centre.”
“Send the report to infrastructure.”
“I’ve sent it four times. The Great Hearing says the readings are still within the compensation range.”
“Then they are.”
Oru switched off the projection and looked at her with his whole attention. For a nivar, this meant turning the head almost squarely towards someone and giving up half the field of vision. The gesture could be tender or aggressive. With Oru, it was usually a request that she stop hiding inside her profession.
“When did you start talking about the system as though it were the weather?” he asked.
“When I found out how many things break if every official thinks they’re cleverer than the model.”
“And how many break when no one does?”
Nemi looked from one to the other, chewing slowly. Sava did not want the little girl to turn every minor disagreement into a danger signal. She lowered her voice.
“After the Festival, I’ll read the raw data. I promise.”
“You said that after the last Festival too.”
“I didn’t promise then.”
Oru accepted the distinction with a movement of his sail. The morning signal came through the floor: two low pulses, then one long one. The city woke around them. Doors slid open. Water began flowing through the washing pipes. Somewhere a child cried, another laughed, and the footsteps of thousands of inhabitants gathered into a murmur carried through the building’s roots.
The peace of Ivarra had a sound. It was not silence. It was the predictable noise of bodies that knew where they had to go.

The Reflex Therapy Centre occupied an old level of the city, built before ceilings had been lowered to the height considered reassuring. The training room therefore seemed too vast. The lights were buried in the floor, and above them lay darkness. Machines hung there like animals that had not yet learned to come down.
Taren stood in the middle of the circle, his hind paws apart and his arms at his sides.
